Assignment 2: Hand Gesture Recognition [50 Pt]¶

This assignment will be completed in two parts. In Part A you will gain experience gathering your own data set (specifically images of hand gestures), and understand the challenges involved in the data cleaning process. In Part B you will train a convolutional neural network to make classifications on different hand gestures. By the end of this assignment, you should be able to:

  1. Generate and preprocess your own data
  2. Load and split data for training, validation and testing
  3. Train a Convolutional Neural Network
  4. Apply transfer learning to improve your model

Note that for this assignment we will not be providing you with any starter code. You should be able to take the sample code provided in the preparation sample code, previous assignment, and lectures and modify it accordingly to complete the tasks outlined below.

This assignment is based on an assignment developed by Prof. Lisa Zhang.

Individual image file names should follow the convention of student-number_Alphabet_file-number.jpg (e.g. 100343434_A_1.jpg).

Part A. Data Collection [5pt]¶

So far, we have worked with data sets that have been collected, cleaned, and curated by machine learning researchers and practitioners. Datasets like MNIST and CIFAR are often used as toy examples, both by students and by researchers testing new machine learning models.

In the real world, getting a clean data set is never that easy. More than half the work in applying machine learning is finding, gathering, cleaning, and formatting your data set.

The purpose of this assignment is to help you gain experience gathering your own data set, and understand the challenges involved in the data cleaning process.

American Sign Language¶

American Sign Language (ASL) is a complete, complex language that employs signs made by moving the hands combined with facial expressions and postures of the body. It is the primary language of many North Americans who are deaf and is one of several communication options used by people who are deaf or hard-of-hearing.

The hand gestures representing English alphabet are shown below. This assignment focuses on classifying a subset of these hand gesture images using convolutional neural networks. Specifically, given an image of a hand showing one of the letters A-I, we want to detect which letter is being represented.

Generating Data¶

We will produce the images required to assess our models by ourselves. You are required to collect, clean and submit three images each of Americal Sign Language gestures for letters A - I (total of 27 images) Steps involved in data collection

  1. Familiarize yourself with American Sign Language gestures for letters from A - I (9 letters).
  2. Take three pictures at slightly different orientation for each letter gesture using your mobile phone.
  • Ensure adequate lighting while you are capturing the images.
  • Use a white wall as your background.
  • Use your right hand to create gestures (for consistency).
  • Keep your right hand fairly apart from your body and any other obstructions.
  • Avoid having shadows on parts of your hand.
  1. Transfer the images to your laptop for cleaning.

Cleaning Data¶

To simplify the machine learning the task, we will standardize the training images. We will make sure that all our images are of the same size (224 x 224 pixels RGB), and have the hand in the center of the cropped regions.

You may use the following applications to crop and resize your images:

Mac

  • Use Preview: – Holding down CMD + Shift will keep a square aspect ratio while selecting the hand area. – Resize to 224x224 pixels.

Windows 10

  • Use Photos app to edit and crop the image and keep the aspect ratio a square.
  • Use Paint to resize the image to the final image size of 224x224 pixels.

Linux

  • You can use GIMP, imagemagick, or other tools of your choosing. You may also use online tools such as http://picresize.com All the above steps are illustrative only. You need not follow these steps but following these will ensure that you produce a good quality dataset. You will be judged based on the quality of the images alone. Please do not edit your photos in any other way. You should not need to change the aspect ratio of your image. You also should not digitally remove the background or shadows—instead, take photos with a white background and minimal shadows.

Accepted Images¶

Images will be accepted and graded based on the criteria below

  1. The final image should be size 224x224 pixels (RGB).
  2. The file format should be a .jpg file.
  3. The hand should be approximately centered on the frame.
  4. The hand should not be obscured or cut off.
  5. The photos follows the ASL gestures posted earlier.
  6. The photos were not edited in any other way (e.g. no electronic removal of shadows or background).

  2. Zip all the images together and name it with the following convention: last-name_student-number.zip (e.g. last-name_100343434.zip).

# Data Loading

import os
import numpy as np
import torch
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, Subset
from torchvision import datasets, transforms
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit
import copy

device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
print("Using device:", device)

def get_data_loader(data_dir, batch_size, valid_split=0.15):
    """
    Load the Gesture Recognition Dataset, split into training, validation, and testing.

    Args:
        data_dir: The root directory of the dataset, with subdirectories for each class.
        batch_size: Number of samples per batch.
        valid_split: Fraction of the data to be used for validation (default: 0.15).

    Returns:
        train_loader: Iterable DataLoader for training data.
        val_loader: Iterable DataLoader for validation data.
        test_loader: Iterable DataLoader for testing data.
        classes: List of class names.
    """
    # Define transformations
    transform = transforms.Compose([
        transforms.Resize((224, 224)),  # Resize to 224x224
        transforms.ToTensor(),         # Convert to Tensor
        transforms.Normalize(mean=[0.485, 0.456, 0.406], std=[0.229, 0.224, 0.225])  # Normalize
    ])

    # Load the full dataset
    dataset = datasets.ImageFolder(data_dir, transform=transform)
    classes = dataset.classes  # Get class names

    # Extract person groups from filenames for group-based splitting
    paths = np.array([p for p, _ in dataset.samples])
    y = np.array([c for _, c in dataset.samples], dtype=np.int64)

    # Extract person ID from filename (e.g., "100_A_1.jpg" -> "100")
    groups = np.array([int(os.path.basename(p).split("_")[0]) for p in paths], dtype=np.int64)

    idx_all = np.arange(len(dataset))

    # Split the dataset by person (group-based split)
    # First split: separate test set (15% of persons)
    test_split = 0.15
    gss1 = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, test_size=test_split, random_state=1000)
    trainval_idx, test_idx = next(gss1.split(idx_all, y, groups))

    # Second split: separate validation set from remaining data
    val_ratio_rel = valid_split / (1 - test_split)  # Relative ratio within trainval
    gss2 = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, test_size=val_ratio_rel, random_state=1000)
    train_rel, val_rel = next(gss2.split(trainval_idx, y[trainval_idx], groups[trainval_idx]))

    train_idx = trainval_idx[train_rel]
    val_idx = trainval_idx[val_rel]


    # Verify no person overlap
    train_persons = set(groups[train_idx])
    val_persons = set(groups[val_idx])
    test_persons = set(groups[test_idx])

    assert len(train_persons & val_persons) == 0, "Person overlap between train-val"
    assert len(train_persons & test_persons) == 0, "Person overlap between train-test"
    assert len(val_persons & test_persons) == 0, "Person overlap between val-test"
    print(f"No person overlap. Train: {len(train_persons)}, Val: {len(val_persons)}, Test: {len(test_persons)} persons")



    # Create dataset subsets
    train_dataset = Subset(dataset, train_idx)
    val_dataset = Subset(dataset, val_idx)
    test_dataset = Subset(dataset, test_idx)

    # Create DataLoaders
    train_loader = DataLoader(train_dataset, batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=True, num_workers=0)
    val_loader = DataLoader(val_dataset, batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=False, num_workers=0)
    test_loader = DataLoader(test_dataset, batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=False, num_workers=0)

    return train_loader, val_loader, test_loader, classes

###############################################################################
# Training

def get_model_name(name, batch_size, learning_rate, epoch):
    """ Generate a name for the model consisting of all the hyperparameter values

    Args:
        name: Name of the model
        batch_size: Batch size used for training
        learning_rate: Learning rate used for training
        epoch: Current epoch number
    Returns:
        path: A string with the hyperparameter name and value concatenated
    """
    path = "model_{0}_bs{1}_lr{2}_epoch{3}".format(name,batch_size,learning_rate, epoch)

    return path

def normalize_label(labels):
    """
    Normalize labels for multi-class classification.

    Args:
        labels: A 1D tensor of scalar class labels.
    Returns:
        The same labels (already suitable for multi-class classification).
    """
    return labels

def evaluate(net, loader, criterion, device):
    """ Evaluate the network on a given dataset.

    Args:
        loader: PyTorch DataLoader for validation data.
        criterion: The loss function.
        device: The device (cpu or cuda) to perform calculations on.

    Returns:
       err: Average classification error rate over the dataset.
       avg_loss: Average loss per sample.
       acc: Average classification accuracy over the dataset.
    """
    net.eval()
    total_loss = 0.0
    total_err = 0
    total_correct = 0
    total_samples = 0

    with torch.no_grad():
        for inputs, labels in loader:
            inputs = inputs.to(device)
            labels = labels.to(device)
            outputs = net(inputs)

            # Compute loss
            loss = criterion(outputs, labels)

            # Compute classification error
            preds = outputs.argmax(dim=1)
            bs = labels.size(0)

            total_loss += loss.item() * bs
            total_err += (preds != labels).sum().item()
            total_correct += (preds == labels).sum().item() # count predictions
            total_samples += bs

    err = total_err / total_samples
    avg_loss = total_loss / total_samples
    acc = total_correct / total_samples
    return err, avg_loss, acc

###############################################################################
# Training Curve

def plot_training_curve(path, return_val_error=False):
    """ Plot training and validation error/loss curves.

    Args:
        path: Base path for the CSV files containing training logs.
        return_val_error: If True, return the final validation error.
    """
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
    import numpy as np

    train_err = np.loadtxt(f"{path}_train_err.csv")
    val_err = np.loadtxt(f"{path}_val_err.csv")
    train_loss = np.loadtxt(f"{path}_train_loss.csv")
    val_loss = np.loadtxt(f"{path}_val_loss.csv")

    if return_val_error:
        return val_err[-1]  # Return the final validation error

    plt.figure()
    plt.title("Train vs Validation Error")
    plt.plot(range(1, len(train_err) + 1), train_err, label="Train")
    plt.plot(range(1, len(val_err) + 1), val_err, label="Validation")
    plt.xlabel("Epoch")
    plt.ylabel("Error")
    plt.legend(loc='best')
    plt.show()

    plt.figure()
    plt.title("Train vs Validation Loss")
    plt.plot(range(1, len(train_loss) + 1), train_loss, label="Train")
    plt.plot(range(1, len(val_loss) + 1), val_loss, label="Validation")
    plt.xlabel("Epoch")
    plt.ylabel("Loss")
    plt.legend(loc='best')
    plt.show()

Part 2. Model Building and Sanity Checking [4pt]¶

Part (i) Convolutional Network [2pt MODEL]¶

Build a convolutional neural network model that takes the (224x224 RGB) image as input, and predicts the gesture letter. Your model should be a subclass of nn.Module. Explain your choice of neural network architecture: how many layers did you choose? What types of layers did you use? Were they fully-connected or convolutional? What about other decisions like pooling layers, activation functions, number of channels / hidden units?

In [7]:
import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
import torch.optim as optim
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, Subset
In [8]:
class CNN(nn.Module):
    """
    CNN for gesture recognition.
    Input:  224x224 RGB images, (B, 3, 224, 224)
    Output: 9 classes (A-I), (B, 9) logits
    """
    def __init__(self, num_classes=9, dropout_p=0.0):
        super().__init__()
        self.name = "CNN"


        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(3, 32, kernel_size=5)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(32, 64, kernel_size=5)
        self.conv3 = nn.Conv2d(64, 128, kernel_size=3)
        self.pool = nn.MaxPool2d(2, 2)

        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(128 * 25 * 25, 512)  #25x25
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(512, 128)
        self.fc3 = nn.Linear(128, num_classes)

        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(p=dropout_p)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.pool(F.relu(self.conv1(x)))  # 224->220->110
        x = self.pool(F.relu(self.conv2(x)))  # 110->106->53
        x = self.pool(F.relu(self.conv3(x)))  # 53->51->25

        x = torch.flatten(x, 1) # (B, 128*28*28)
        x = self.dropout(F.relu(self.fc1(x)))
        x = self.dropout(F.relu(self.fc2(x)))
        logits = self.fc3(x)   # (B, 9)
        return logits

'''
PROVIDE YOUR ANSWER BELOW

Explain your choice of neural network architecture: how many layers did you choose? What types of layers did you use?
Were they fully-connected or convolutional? What about other decisions like pooling layers, activation functions, number of channels / hidden units?


A classic Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) with 3 layers is used here.
I chose convolutional layers for the initial stages. With the use of kernel, these layers are ideal for capturing patterns
like edges and curves of the hand. Also, convolutional layers are translation-invariant. This means that the model will be
able to identify a gesture regardless of its location in the 224x224 pixels, which is a much more efficient solution than using
a fully connected network on pixels alone.

I also used 3 fully-connected layers at the end to serve as the classifier. They take the high-level abstract features from previous convolutional layers,
and classify them to the final 9 classes (A-I).

Besides layer settings, I also applied Max Pooling after each convolutional layer. This progressively reduces the spatial dimensions,
which helps to reduce computational cost, control overfitting, and make the representation more abstract.

I used the ReLU as an activation function after every learnable layer, except the output layer. ReLU introduces non-linearity to our network,
so it allows the network to learn complex mappings and mitigates the vanishing gradient problem during training compared to Sigmoid or Tanh.

I applied the standard channel setting for the network. Since the input images are RGB(3x3), the network goes from 3, 32, 64, 128 as the network goes deeper.
This design helps early layers capture simple features as there are fewer channels, while deeper layers capture complex, high-level combinations of features.

For the fc layers, I chose to start off with many units (512) to handle the flattened feature map, then turned it down to 128 before the final output layer,
so that the network can learn to represent the hand gestures in a compressed format.

I also included a Dropout layer in the fully connected stages to randomly zero out neurons during training. By using this regularization technique,
the network can better prevent overfitting to the training data.



'''

Part (ii) Training Code [1pt MODEL]¶

Write code that trains your neural network given some training data. Your training code should make it easy to tweak the usual hyperparameters, like batch size, learning rate, and the model object itself. Make sure that you are checkpointing your models from time to time (the frequency is up to you). Explain your choice of loss function and optimizer.

def train_net(net, train_loader, val_loader, learning_rate=0.001, num_epochs=30,
              save_dir='/content/drive/MyDrive/MIE1517_A2_Data/models',
              weight_decay=0.0, patience=10):


    """
    Train the CNN model on gesture recognition dataset.
    Checkpoints are saved periodically, and training history is saved as CSV.
    """


    # Moving model to GPU
    device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
    print("Using device:", device)
    net = net.to(device)


    # Fixed PyTorch random seed for reproducible results
    torch.manual_seed(1000)

    # Define the Loss function and optimizer
    # Use CrossEntropyLoss for multi-class classification
    criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
    optimizer = optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr=learning_rate, weight_decay=weight_decay)



    # Set up some numpy arrays to store the training/test loss/accuracy
    train_err  = np.zeros(num_epochs)
    train_loss = np.zeros(num_epochs)
    train_acc  = np.zeros(num_epochs)
    val_err    = np.zeros(num_epochs)
    val_loss   = np.zeros(num_epochs)
    val_acc    = np.zeros(num_epochs)

    os.makedirs(save_dir, exist_ok=True)

    # Initialize early stopping parameters
    best_val_loss = np.inf
    best_epoch = 0
    best_state = None
    bad_epochs = 0
    min_delta = 0.0001 # Minimum change to be considered an improvement

    # Train the network # Loop over the data iterator and sample a new batch of training data
    # Get the output from the network, and optimize our loss function.
    import time
    start_time = time.time()

    for epoch in range(num_epochs):
        net.train()

        total_train_loss = 0.0
        total_train_err = 0
        total_correct = 0
        total_samples = 0

        for inputs, labels in train_loader:
            inputs = inputs.to(device)
            labels = labels.to(device)

            optimizer.zero_grad()
            outputs = net(inputs)
            loss = criterion(outputs, labels)
            loss.backward()
            optimizer.step()

            preds = outputs.argmax(dim=1)
            bs = labels.size(0)

            total_train_err += (preds != labels).sum().item()
            total_correct   += (preds == labels).sum().item()
            total_train_loss += loss.item() * bs
            total_samples += bs



        # Calculate error, loss, accuracy for the training and validation set
        train_err[epoch]  = total_train_err / total_samples
        train_loss[epoch] = total_train_loss / total_samples
        train_acc[epoch]  = total_correct / total_samples

        val_err[epoch], val_loss[epoch], val_acc[epoch] = evaluate(net, val_loader, criterion, device)
        # val_acc[epoch] = 1.0 - val_err[epoch] # This line was incorrect as evaluate now returns acc directly


        # Print stats for the current epoch
        print(
            f"Epoch {epoch + 1}/{num_epochs}: "
            f"Train acc: {train_acc[epoch]:.4f}, err: {train_err[epoch]:.4f}, loss: {train_loss[epoch]:.4f} | "
            f"Val acc: {val_acc[epoch]:.4f}, err: {val_err[epoch]:.4f}, loss: {val_loss[epoch]:.4f}"
        )


        # Early stopping logic
        if val_loss[epoch] < best_val_loss - min_delta:
            best_val_loss = val_loss[epoch]
            best_epoch = epoch + 1
            best_state = copy.deepcopy(net.state_dict())
            bad_epochs = 0
        else:
            bad_epochs += 1
            if bad_epochs >= patience:
                print(f"Early stopping: no val_loss improvement for {patience} epochs. Best epoch = {best_epoch}")
                break

    elapsed_time = time.time() - start_time
    print(f"Finished Training. Total time elapsed: {elapsed_time:.2f} seconds")


    # Load the best weights before returning
    if best_state is not None:
        print(f"Restoring model weights from Best Epoch {best_epoch}")
        net.load_state_dict(best_state)

    # Save history
    bs = train_loader.batch_size
    base = os.path.join(save_dir, f"{net.name}_bs{bs}_lr{learning_rate:g}_wd{weight_decay:g}")
    np.savetxt(f"{base}_train_err.csv", train_err)
    np.savetxt(f"{base}_train_loss.csv", train_loss)
    np.savetxt(f"{base}_train_acc.csv", train_acc)
    np.savetxt(f"{base}_val_err.csv", val_err)
    np.savetxt(f"{base}_val_loss.csv", val_loss)
    np.savetxt(f"{base}_val_acc.csv", val_acc)

    return net, {
        "train_err": train_err, "train_loss": train_loss, "train_acc": train_acc,
        "val_err": val_err, "val_loss": val_loss, "val_acc": val_acc,
        "best_epoch": best_epoch, "best_val_loss": best_val_loss # Added best_epoch and best_val_loss
    }

Part (iii) “Overfit” to a Small Dataset - [1pt MODEL]¶

One way to sanity check our neural network model and training code is to check whether the model is capable of “overfitting” or “memorizing” a small dataset. A properly constructed CNN with correct training code should be able to memorize the answers to a small number of images quickly.

Construct a small dataset (e.g. just the images that you have collected). Then show that your model and training code is capable of memorizing the labels of this small data set.

With a large batch size (e.g. the entire small dataset) and learning rate that is not too high, you should be able to obtain a 100% training accuracy on that small dataset relatively quickly (within 200 iterations).

In [ ]:
# TO BE COMPLETED

device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

#pick a small subset from training dataset
# train_loader.dataset is a Subset(ImageFolder, train_idx)
base_train_ds = train_loader.dataset
n_small = 45  # e.g. 45 images total
small_indices = np.random.RandomState(0).choice(len(base_train_ds), size=n_small, replace=False)

small_ds = Subset(base_train_ds, small_indices)
small_loader = DataLoader(small_ds, batch_size=len(small_ds), shuffle=True)  # full-batch

print("Small dataset size:", len(small_ds))

# new model (fresh) + optimizer + loss
net_small = CNN(num_classes=9).to(device)
criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
optimizer = optim.Adam(net_small.parameters(), lr=1e-3)  # not too high

#train for <=200 iterations
max_iters = 200
net_small.train()

for it in range(1, max_iters + 1):
    inputs, labels = next(iter(small_loader))  # one full batch
    inputs, labels = inputs.to(device), labels.to(device)

    optimizer.zero_grad()
    outputs = net_small(inputs)
    loss = criterion(outputs, labels)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

    with torch.no_grad():
        acc = (outputs.argmax(dim=1) == labels).float().mean().item()

    if it % 10 == 0 or acc == 1.0:
        print(f"Iteration {it:3d}: loss={loss.item():.4f}, train_acc={acc:.4f}")

    if acc == 1.0:
        print(f"Reached 100% training accuracy in {it} iterations.")
        break

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

def plot_training_results(hist):
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
    import numpy as np

    n = len(hist["train_loss"])
    epochs = np.arange(1, n + 1)

    plt.figure(figsize=(18, 5))

    plt.subplot(1, 3, 1)
    plt.plot(epochs, hist["train_loss"], label="Train Loss")
    plt.plot(epochs, hist["val_loss"], label="Val Loss")
    plt.title("Loss")
    plt.xlabel("Epoch"); plt.ylabel("Loss")
    plt.legend(); plt.grid(True)

    plt.subplot(1, 3, 2)
    plt.plot(epochs, hist["train_acc"], label="Train Acc")
    plt.plot(epochs, hist["val_acc"], label="Val Acc")
    plt.title("Accuracy")
    plt.xlabel("Epoch"); plt.ylabel("Acc")
    plt.legend(); plt.grid(True)

    plt.subplot(1, 3, 3)
    plt.plot(epochs, hist["train_err"], label="Train Err")
    plt.plot(epochs, hist["val_err"], label="Val Err")
    plt.title("Error")
    plt.xlabel("Epoch"); plt.ylabel("Err")
    plt.legend(); plt.grid(True)

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

likely too aggressive; it constrains the model's capacity to learn.

def get_predictions(net, loader, device):
    all_preds = []
    all_labels = []
    net.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        for inputs, labels in loader:
            inputs = inputs.to(device)
            labels = labels.to(device)
            outputs = net(inputs)
            preds = outputs.argmax(dim=1)
            all_preds.extend(preds.cpu().numpy())
            all_labels.extend(labels.cpu().numpy())
    return np.array(all_preds), np.array(all_labels)

preds, targets = get_predictions(model, test_loader, device)

Part 4. Transfer Learning [8pt]¶

For many image classification tasks, it is generally not a good idea to train a very large deep neural network model from scratch due to the enormous compute requirements and lack of sufficient amounts of training data.

One of the better options is to try using an existing model that performs a similar task to the one you need to solve. This method of utilizing a pre-trained network for other similar tasks is broadly termed Transfer Learning. In this assignment, we will use Transfer Learning to extract features from the hand gesture images. Then, train a smaller network to use these features as input and classify the hand gestures.

As you have learned from the CNN lecture, convolution layers extract various features from the images which get utilized by the fully connected layers for correct classification. AlexNet architecture played a pivotal role in establishing Deep Neural Nets as a go-to tool for image classification problems and we will use an ImageNet pre-trained AlexNet model to extract features in this assignment.

Part (i) - [1pt EXPLORATORY]¶

Here is the code to load the AlexNet network, with pretrained weights. When you first run the code, PyTorch will download the pretrained weights from the internet.

The alexnet model is split up into two components: alexnet.features and alexnet.classifier. The first neural network component, alexnet.features, is used to compute convolutional features, which are taken as input in alexnet.classifier.

The neural network alexnet.features expects an image tensor of shape Nx3x224x224 as input and it will output a tensor of shape Nx256x6x6 . (N = batch size).

Compute the AlexNet features for each of your training, validation, and test data. Here is an example code snippet showing how you can compute the AlexNet features for some images (your actual code might be different):

In [ ]:
# img = ... a PyTorch tensor with shape [N,3,224,224] containing hand images ...
features = alexnet.features(img)

Save the computed features. You will be using these features as input to your neural network in Part (ii), and you do not want to re-compute the features every time. Instead, run alexnet.features once for each image, and save the result.

In [34]:
import os
import torch


device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
alexnet = alexnet.to(device)
alexnet.eval()

def get_features(loader, model, device):
    # Lists to store features and labels
    features_list = []
    labels_list = []

    print(f"Extracting features from {len(loader)} batches...")

    with torch.no_grad():
        for img, label in loader:
            img = img.to(device)
            # Pass image through the convolutional layers (features)
            # Output shape: (Batch_Size, 256, 6, 6)
            feature = model.features(img)

            # Move to CPU to save memory and append
            features_list.append(feature.cpu()) # Detach and move to CPU
            labels_list.append(label)

    # Concatenate all batches
    features = torch.cat(features_list, dim=0)
    labels = torch.cat(labels_list, dim=0)
    return features, labels

# Extract features for all splits
train_features, train_labels = get_features(train_loader, alexnet, device)
val_features, val_labels = get_features(val_loader, alexnet, device)
test_features, test_labels = get_features(test_loader, alexnet, device)

# Save to Drive so we don't have to compute them again

Part (ii) - [1pt MODEL]¶

Build a convolutional neural network that takes as input these AlexNet features, and makes a prediction using additional convolutional and/or linear layers. Your model should be a subclass of nn.Module.

Here is an example of how your model may be called:

In [35]:
class AlexNetFeatureClassifier(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_classes=9):
        super(AlexNetFeatureClassifier, self).__init__()
        self.name = "AlexNetFeatureClassifier"
        # Input features shape from AlexNet: (Batch_Size, 256, 6, 6)

        # Convolutional layer to reduce depth and extract further spatial patterns
        # Input: 256 channels, Output: 128 channels
        self.conv = nn.Conv2d(in_channels=256, out_channels=128, kernel_size=3, padding=1)

        # Fully connected layers
        # Flattened size: 128 * 6 * 6 = 4608
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(128 * 6 * 6, 512)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(512, num_classes)

        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(0.3)

    def forward(self, x):
        # x shape: [B, 256, 6, 6]
        x = F.relu(self.conv(x))

        # Flatten
        x = x.view(-1, 128 * 6 * 6)

        x = self.dropout(F.relu(self.fc1(x)))
        x = self.fc2(x)
        return x

# Verify model architecture
model_alex = AlexNetFeatureClassifier()
print(model_alex)

# Sanity check with dummy input
dummy_input = torch.randn(2, 256, 6, 6)
print("Output shape:", model_alex(dummy_input).shape)

AlexNetFeatureClassifier(
  (conv): Conv2d(256, 128, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
  (fc1): Linear(in_features=4608, out_features=512, bias=True)
  (fc2): Linear(in_features=512, out_features=9, bias=True)
  (dropout): Dropout(p=0.3, inplace=False)
)

#Extract Features (Re-using the logic from Part 4(i))
def get_resnet_features(loader, model, device):
    features_list = []
    labels_list = []
    print(f"Extracting features from {len(loader)} batches")
    with torch.no_grad():
        for img, label in loader:
            img = img.to(device)
            feature = model(img)
            features_list.append(feature.cpu())
            labels_list.append(label)
    return torch.cat(features_list, dim=0), torch.cat(labels_list, dim=0)

In [ ]:






class ResNetFeatureClassifier(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_classes=9):
        super(ResNetFeatureClassifier, self).__init__()
        self.name = "ResNetFeatureClassifier"
        # Input shape: (Batch_Size, 512, 1, 1)

        # 1x1 Convolution: Effectively acts as a dense layer but satisfies "CNN" definition
        # Reduces channels from 512 -> 256
        self.conv = nn.Conv2d(in_channels=512, out_channels=256, kernel_size=1)

        # Flatten: (B, 256, 1, 1) -> (B, 256)
        # The spatial dimensions are already 1x1, so this just removes them
        self.fc = nn.Linear(256, num_classes)

        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(0.3)

    def forward(self, x):
        # x: (B, 512, 1, 1)
        x = F.relu(self.conv(x))

        x = x.view(x.size(0), -1) # Flatten

        x = self.dropout(x)
        x = self.fc(x)
        return x

# Sanity Check
model_res = ResNetFeatureClassifier()
print(model_res)
dummy = torch.randn(2, 512, 1, 1)
print("Output shape:", model_res(dummy).shape)

)

'''
PROVIDE YOUR ANSWER BELOW

Comparison:
While both pretrained models had significantly higher accuracy than the custom CNN from Part 3 (79%),
AlexNet (96.51%) performed better than ResNet18 (90.32%).

The result is interesting since ResNet is considered as a newer and stronger net than AlexNet, but in the current experiment, the result is out of this expectation.

Discussion:
In hand gesture recognition, spatial information, such as the specific location of fingers relative to the palm, is important for distinguishing between similar classes.
Just like Class A and Class E, the two classes that were often hard to distinguish by the model. Both involve a compact, closed-fist structure, making them hard to
differentiate. If we consider from the model perspective, they share similar low-level visual features. Therefore, if the model has less ability in preserving spatial
grid information, it would be more likely that this model predicts the incorrect hand guesture.

AlexNet's feature output is 6x6, this output preserve the spatial information, the image is not fully flattened like in ResNet, which output is 1x1.
Therefore, the spatial preserving advantage in AlexNet's output help it achieve better performance than ResNet.



'''

import zipfile
from PIL import Image
import torch
from torch.utils.data import Dataset, DataLoader
from torchvision import transforms
import glob

#Unzip the file
zip_path = '/content/Xu_1007901512.zip'
extract_path = '/content/my_data'

if os.path.exists(zip_path):
    print(f"Unzipping {zip_path}")
    with zipfile.ZipFile(zip_path, 'r') as zip_ref:
        zip_ref.extractall(extract_path)
else:
    print(f"Error: {zip_path} not found. ")

#Define Custom Dataset
class MyGestureDataset(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, root_dir, transform=None):
        self.root_dir = root_dir
        self.transform = transform
        # Find all .jpg images recursively
        self.image_paths = sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(root_dir, '**', '*.jpg'), recursive=True))
        self.classes = ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'E', 'F', 'G', 'H', 'I']
        self.class_to_idx = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(self.classes)}

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.image_paths)

    def __getitem__(self, idx):
        img_path = self.image_paths[idx]
        image = Image.open(img_path).convert('RGB')

        filename = os.path.basename(img_path)
        try:
            # Split by '_' and take the second part
            label_str = filename.split('_')[1]
            label = self.class_to_idx[label_str]
        except (IndexError, KeyError):
            print(f"Warning: Could not parse label from {filename}, skipping")
            label = 0 # Default fallback

        if self.transform:
            image = self.transform(image)

        return image, label

#Create DataLoader
# Use exactly the same transform as training
my_transform = transforms.Compose([
    transforms.Resize((224, 224)),
    transforms.ToTensor(),
    transforms.Normalize(mean=[0.485, 0.456, 0.406], std=[0.229, 0.224, 0.225])
])

my_dataset = MyGestureDataset(root_dir=extract_path, transform=my_transform)
my_loader = DataLoader(my_dataset, batch_size=32, shuffle=False)

print(f"Successfully loaded {len(my_dataset)} images from Part A.")

#Define Unlabeled Dataset
class UnlabeledDataset(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, root_dir, transform=None):
        self.root_dir = root_dir
        self.transform = transform
        self.image_paths = sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(root_dir, '**', '*.jpg'), recursive=True))

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.image_paths)

    def __getitem__(self, idx):
        img_path = self.image_paths[idx]
        image = Image.open(img_path).convert('RGB')

        # Extract ID from filename (e.g. "123.jpg" -> 123)
        filename = os.path.basename(img_path)
        # Use regex to find the number in the filename
        match = re.search(r'(\d+)', filename)
        if match:
            img_id = int(match.group(1))
        else:
            img_id = -1 # Should not happen based on description

        if self.transform:
            image = self.transform(image)

        return image, img_id

'''
PROVIDE YOUR ANSWER BELOW

The performance of all models are dropped.

Performance on My data:
  The transfered AlexNet achieved an accuracy of 74.07%, which is a significant drop from its original test accuracy of 96.51%.
  The custom CNN from Part 3 achieved 70.37%, which has a much smaller relative drop from its original 79.57%.
  While the Transfer Learning model still perform better than the custom CNN, it demostrates a much more severe performance degradation
  when exposed to completely unseen data. This indicates that while transfer learning is powerful, it is not immune to domain shifts.

Domain Shift:
  This idea means the training data and the new data look different. The background, lighting, and camera can change. So the model may not generalize well.
  The change between the model's accuracy on the original data set and my own hand data set would be explained by this idea.
  The models were trained on a specific "source domain" (the original dataset), which likely had consistent patterns that were captured by the two models.
  My collected data represents a "target domain" with different environmental factors. For AlexNet's huge drop on accuracy may indicate AlexNet could have overfit the particular details of the source domain.
  High-capacity models tend to learn to exploit the particular, non-robust details of the source domain that allow it to reach near-perfect accuracy. However, when these details are not present in my personal data,
  the model fails to generalize well, resulting in a drastic drop in performance. This is an interesting observation because, despite applying Dropout to the model, the domain shift problem still exists.


Real world application:
If this model were to be deployed in a real-world application, its current performance on new data would not likely to be well performed for a smooth user experience.
Users would experience frequent misclassifications if their lighting or background didn't match the training data perfectly. It could be a burden for their lives.

To address these limitations and improve the model's robustness for real-world deployment, we should bridge the domain gap between the clean training environment and chaotic real-world scenarios.

    First, we can use data augmentation, but in a more aggressive mode during training, since we believe the AlexNet is overfitting, to have the dropped accuracy.
    Data augmentation is a great way to manage this issue. By applying transformations such as random rotations, color jittering, and background substitution,
    we can force the model to learn features that are invariant to lighting changes and environmental clutter.

    Second, the training data itself should be augmented to cover various images that depict different skin tones, camera views, and lighting setups,
    making the model less dependent on source-domain features.

    Lastly, instead of relying on the fixed feature extractor, fine-tuning the pre-trained model by unfreezing the convolutional layers would enable the network to learn its feature
    extractors specifically for hand structural patterns, as opposed to the general ImageNet features, thus greatly improving its generalization performance.

Reflect on the ethical implications of deploying a hand gesture recognition model in real-world applications. What are some potential biases that could arise in your model, and how might they impact different user groups?


Discuss measures you can take to identify and mitigate these biases during the development and deployment phases. Consider aspects such as data collection, model training, and user feedback.


















In [ ]:






'''
PROVIDE YOUR ANSWER BELOW

If applying this model in real-world,

The potential biases could be:

1. Skin Tone Bias: the dataset used for this assignment or many other public dataset tend to not represent darker skin tones or particular
  lighting conditions that affect the reflection of light on the skin. A model trained on mostly lighter skin tone data might not correctly identify
  gestures from users with darker skin. This could create a discriminatory user experience, which can have serious consequence.
  To mitigate this, we should intentionally collect more diverse datasets across skin tones and lighting, then evaluate performance with subgroup metrics,
  such as accuracy/FNR by skin tone and illumination, and apply targeted augmentations (brightness/contrast, shadows) or re-weighting to reduce performance gaps.

2. Privacy: using a hand gesture recognition model would often require users to turn on their cameras, and it could involve privacy issue.
   One of the biggest risks in privacy is the discrepancy between what the users assume is captured by the camera and what actually is captured.
   Many times, in many applications, the UI may only show or indicate the camera is capturing part of an image or video, for example, only the hand area.
   However, the opposite may actually be captured by the camera, like the faces or surroundings, and the cropping may only be done on the camera in the video or image itself.
   To solve this problem, the application should clearly indicate what is captured by the camera, reduce the risk of collection, and clearly show users when recording is active.

3. Hand gesture recognition is more likely to be used for accessibility contexts, such as helping with hearing or speaking difficulties populations.
   However, users may vary in dexterity and range of motion due to injuries, arthritis, tremors, or limb differences. If the model is trained mostly with "ideal" gesture forms,
   it may have systematic misrecognition of such users as an accessibility barrier. To address this bias, we should make sure that our dataset
   contains a variety of different gesture variations in order to evaluate the performance of users with mobility profiles that could result from a wide
   variety of factors when ethically appropriate.




'''

# Task 1: Stress Test
import glob, os, random
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from PIL import Image
from torch.utils.data import Dataset, DataLoader
from torchvision import transforms, models
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix

# 1. Setup & Model Definition
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

transform = transforms.Compose([
    transforms.Resize((224, 224)),
    transforms.ToTensor(),
    transforms.Normalize(mean=[0.485, 0.456, 0.406], std=[0.229, 0.224, 0.225])
])

class AlexNetFeatureClassifier(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_classes=9):
        super(AlexNetFeatureClassifier, self).__init__()
        self.conv = nn.Conv2d(256, 128, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(128 * 6 * 6, 512)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(512, num_classes)
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(0.3)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = F.relu(self.conv(x))
        x = x.view(-1, 128 * 6 * 6)
        x = self.dropout(F.relu(self.fc1(x)))
        x = self.fc2(x)
        return x

# Load Weights
alexnet = models.alexnet(pretrained=True).to(device).eval()
model_bonus = AlexNetFeatureClassifier(num_classes=9).to(device)
model_bonus.load_state_dict(torch.load('part4.pt', map_location=device))
model_bonus.eval()

classes = ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'E', 'F', 'G', 'H', 'I']

# 2. Dataset
class StressTestDataset(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, root_dir, transform=None):
        self.image_paths = sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(root_dir, '**', '*.jpg'), recursive=True) +
                                  glob.glob(os.path.join(root_dir, '**', '*.jpeg'), recursive=True))
        self.transform = transform
    def __len__(self): return len(self.image_paths)
    def __getitem__(self, idx):
        path = self.image_paths[idx]
        img = Image.open(path).convert('RGB')
        label = os.path.basename(path).split('_')[0]
        if label not in classes: label = os.path.basename(os.path.dirname(path))
        if self.transform: img = self.transform(img)
        return img, label, path

# 3. Execution
target_dir = '/content/asl_alphabet_test'
dataset = StressTestDataset(root_dir=target_dir, transform=transform)
loader = DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=32, shuffle=False)

all_preds, all_labels = [], []
with torch.no_grad():
    for images, raw_labels, _ in loader:
        images = images.to(device)
        outputs = model_bonus(alexnet.features(images))
        _, preds = torch.max(F.softmax(outputs, dim=1), dim=1)
        for i in range(len(images)):
            all_preds.append(classes[preds[i].item()])
            all_labels.append(raw_labels[i])

# 4. Results
correct = sum([t == p for t, p in zip(all_labels, all_preds)])
print(f"Stress Test Accuracy: {correct/len(all_labels):.2%} ({correct}/{len(all_labels)})\n")

cm = confusion_matrix(all_labels, all_preds, labels=classes)
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
sns.heatmap(pd.DataFrame(cm, index=classes, columns=classes), annot=True, fmt='d', cmap='Reds')
plt.xlabel("Predicted"); plt.ylabel("True"); plt.title("Confusion Matrix (Complex Backgrounds)")
plt.show()

#Task 2:

import cv2
import numpy as np
import os
import glob
from tqdm import tqdm
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def gen_noise_bg(shape):
    return np.random.randint(0, 255, shape, dtype=np.uint8)

def gen_gradient_bg(shape):
    h, w, c = shape
    img = np.zeros((h, w, c), dtype=np.uint8)
    c1 = np.random.randint(0, 255, 3)
    c2 = np.random.randint(0, 255, 3)

    # Linear interpolation
    for i in range(h):
        alpha = i / h
        color = (1 - alpha) * c1 + alpha * c2
        img[i, :, :] = color
    return img

def gen_checker_bg(shape):
    """
    Generates a checkerboard pattern.

    """
    h, w, c = shape
    img = np.zeros((h, w, c), dtype=np.uint8)
    sq_size = np.random.randint(20, 50)  # Randomize square size
    c1 = np.random.randint(0, 255, 3)
    c2 = np.random.randint(0, 255, 3)

    for y in range(0, h, sq_size):
        for x in range(0, w, sq_size):
            if ((x // sq_size) + (y // sq_size)) % 2 == 0:
                img[y:y+sq_size, x:x+sq_size] = c1
            else:
                img[y:y+sq_size, x:x+sq_size] = c2
    return img[:h, :w, :]

def augment_image(image_path, save_path):
    """
    Reads an image, segments the hand using HSV,
    and swaps the background.

    """
    img = cv2.imread(image_path)
    if img is None:
        return None

    img = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)

    # Convert to HSV for better skin/background separation
    hsv = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_RGB2HSV)

    # Define threshold for white background
    # (Low saturation, High value usually indicates white/bright background)
    lower_white = np.array([0, 0, 200])
    upper_white = np.array([180, 50, 255])

    # Create binary mask: 1 for BG, 0 for Hand
    bg_mask = cv2.inRange(hsv, lower_white, upper_white)

    # Clean up the mask using morphological operations
    kernel = np.ones((5,5), np.uint8)
    bg_mask = cv2.dilate(bg_mask, kernel, iterations=2)
    bg_mask = cv2.GaussianBlur(bg_mask, (5, 5), 0)

    # Invert to get hand mask
    hand_mask = cv2.bitwise_not(bg_mask)
    mask_norm = hand_mask[:, :, None] / 255.0

    # Generate a random background
    generators = [gen_noise_bg, gen_gradient_bg, gen_checker_bg]
    chosen_bg = np.random.choice(generators)(img.shape)

    # Composite: Hand * Mask + NewBG * (1 - Mask)
    final_img = (img * mask_norm + chosen_bg * (1 - mask_norm)).astype(np.uint8)

    # Save result (convert back to BGR for OpenCV)
    final_img_bgr = cv2.cvtColor(final_img, cv2.COLOR_RGB2BGR)
    cv2.imwrite(save_path, final_img_bgr)

    return img, final_img

# Main execution block
source_dir = '/content/local_data/Lab_3b_Gesture_Dataset Revised'
output_dir = '/content/augmented_data'

print(f"Source: {source_dir}")
print(f"Target: {output_dir}")

# Find all images
all_images = glob.glob(os.path.join(source_dir, '**', '*.jpg'), recursive=True)

if not all_images:
    print("No images found. Please check the source directory.")
else:
    samples = []

    # Process images with progress bar
    for i, path in enumerate(tqdm(all_images, desc="Processing")):
        # Replicate directory structure
        rel_path = os.path.relpath(path, source_dir)
        out_path = os.path.join(output_dir, rel_path)
        os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(out_path), exist_ok=True)

        # Augment
        original, augmented = augment_image(path, out_path)

        # Save a few examples for visualization later
        if i % 500 == 0 and augmented is not None:
            samples.append((original, augmented))

    print(f"\nSuccess,Created {len(all_images)} augmented images.")

    # Visualization
    if samples:
        plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
        for i, (orig, aug) in enumerate(samples[:4]):
            # Show Original
            plt.subplot(2, 4, i + 1)
            plt.imshow(orig)
            plt.title("Original")
            plt.axis('off')

            # Show Augmented
            plt.subplot(2, 4, i + 5)
            plt.imshow(aug)
            plt.title("Augmented")
            plt.axis('off')
        plt.tight_layout()
        plt.show()

Assignment Grading Rubric¶
The grading of the assignment will be based on the following categories:


(0) 5 Pt - DATA Generating new data to evaluate your model.


(1) 9 Pt - EXPLORATORY QUESTIONS These are basic questions that in most cases can be answered without requiring a fully working and trained neural network model. For example, data loading, processing and visualization, summary statistics, data exploration, model and training setup, etc.


(2) 9 Pt - MODEL Student has successfully implemented all the required neural network models and has demonstrated successful training of the model without any errors.


(3) 9 Pt - RESULT Students are evaluated based on the results achieved in comparison to the expected results of the assignment.


(4) 9 Pt - DISCUSSION QUESTIONS Student demonstrated understanding beyond the basic exploratory questions, can answer some of the more challenging questions, and provide arguments for their model selection decisions.


(5) 9 Pt - COMMUNICATION Student has provided a quality submission that is easy to read without too many unnecessary output statements that distract the reading of the document. The code has been well commented and all the answers are communicated clearly and concisely.


(6) 5 Pt - BONUS Student has completed the assignment and has taken on the challenging bonus tasks listed in PART C. The student has demonstrated a good understanding of all aspects of the assignment and has exceeded expectations for the assignment.
